title: “Oh LLM, I’m Asking Thee, Please Give Me a Decision Tree”: Zero-Shot Decision Tree Induction and Embedding with Large Language Models

problem.claim: Predictive modeling is challenging when data is limited.

gap.claim: Data-driven machine learning methods lack knowledge-driven baselines for low-data tabular learning.

contributions.claim: A zero-shot approach uses LLM knowledge to generate interpretable decision trees without training data.
The work derives embeddings from zero-shot LLM-induced decision trees.
The approaches are positioned as knowledge-driven baselines for low-data tabular machine learning.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Zero-shot decision trees surpass data-driven trees on some small-sized tabular datasets.
Embeddings derived from zero-shot decision trees perform better than data-driven tree-based embeddings on average.
Code and results are available in a public repository.

narrative_sequence.summary: LLMs can leverage prior knowledge when predictive-modeling data is limited.
LLMs generate interpretable decision trees without training data.
Zero-shot trees and their embeddings are reported to outperform data-driven counterparts in specified aggregate settings.
The approaches can serve as knowledge-driven baselines and harness LLM world knowledge for tabular tasks.
Code and results are reported as available online.

source_observation.claim: Zero-shot LLM-generated decision trees can outperform data-driven trees on some small tabular datasets.

interpretation.claim: Compressed prior knowledge may be useful as a modeling signal when labeled data is scarce.

application.claim: Consider knowledge-driven baselines alongside data-driven methods in low-data tabular settings.

exception.claim: The reported advantage is limited to some small-sized datasets and average embedding performance; broader conditions are unspecified.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the LLMs, prompting procedure, datasets, metrics, or evaluation protocol.
The abstract does not establish performance outside the described small-sized tabular and average embedding settings.
